description: BMR, PAL, energy balance, recommended energy proportions, and how to analyse the nutritional value of a recipe.
content_html:
Where Does Energy Come From — and How Much Do You Need?

Every time you move, breathe, digest food or maintain your body temperature, you use energy. That energy comes from the macronutrients in food: carbohydrates and protein each supply 4 kcal (kilocalories) per gram; fat supplies 9 kcal per gram; alcohol supplies 7 kcal per gram (not on the spec but worth knowing for context). The total energy a person needs each day depends on two factors: their basal metabolic rate (BMR) and their physical activity level.

Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR)

BMR is the energy your body burns at rest — doing nothing but keeping the heart beating, the lungs breathing and the cells functioning. It accounts for roughly 60–75% of total daily energy use. Several factors affect BMR:

  • Age — BMR declines with age as muscle mass decreases and metabolism slows. A 16-year-old has a higher BMR per kilogram of body weight than a 60-year-old.
  • Gender — males typically have higher BMR than females of the same weight because they generally have more muscle mass. Muscle tissue burns more energy at rest than fat tissue.
  • Body composition — a person with more lean muscle mass has a higher BMR. A marathon runner has a higher BMR than a sedentary person of the same weight.
  • Hormones — thyroid hormones regulate metabolic rate; an overactive thyroid raises BMR, an underactive thyroid lowers it.
  • Pregnancy — BMR increases during pregnancy because the body is supporting fetal development and preparing for breastfeeding.
Key Fact

BMR is the energy the body needs at complete rest to maintain vital functions. It is affected by age (declines with age), gender (males typically higher), body composition (more muscle = higher BMR), hormones and life stage (pregnancy increases it). BMR accounts for approximately 60–75% of total daily energy expenditure.

Physical Activity Level (PAL)

Physical activity level (PAL) is a multiplier that reflects how much energy a person uses through movement on top of their BMR. A sedentary adult (desk job, little exercise) has a PAL of roughly 1.4; a moderately active adult (some walking, 3–4 sessions of exercise per week) has a PAL of around 1.6–1.7; a very active person (manual job or elite athlete in daily training) can have a PAL above 1.9.

Total daily energy requirement = BMR × PAL. For example, a 15-year-old girl with a BMR of 1,400 kcal/day who plays netball four times a week and walks to school (PAL ≈ 1.7) needs approximately 2,380 kcal per day. If she eats less than this consistently, she loses weight; if she eats more, she gains weight.

Energy Balance

Energy balance means intake equals expenditure. Positive energy balance (more in than out) leads to weight gain over time, as excess energy is stored as body fat. Negative energy balance (more out than in) leads to weight loss. For a person trying to manage their weight, increasing PAL (more physical activity) or reducing energy-dense food intake are both effective strategies.

A common misconception is that eating fat directly causes weight gain while eating carbohydrate does not. In reality, weight gain comes from positive energy balance — consuming more total kilocalories than you expend. Fat contributes more kcal per gram (9 kcal/g vs 4 kcal/g for carbohydrate or protein), so high-fat foods are energy-dense and easy to overconsume. But a diet high in refined carbohydrates and sugar can equally lead to positive energy balance and weight gain. The focus should be on total energy intake relative to PAL, not on demonising any single macronutrient.

Recommended Percentages of Energy from Nutrients

Current guidelines specify that the balance of macronutrients in the diet should be:

  • Protein: 15% of total energy intake.
  • Fat: 35% or less of total energy intake (of which no more than 11% from saturated fats).
  • Carbohydrate: 50% of total energy intake — of which 45% from starches, lactose in milk and fruit sugars, and a maximum of 5% from free sugars (added sugars, honey, syrups and fruit juices).

These are percentage targets for the whole diet over time, not for every individual meal. In practice, a typical UK diet has too many free sugars and saturated fats and not enough dietary fibre. A dinner of grilled salmon (protein and unsaturated fat), a large portion of brown rice (complex carbohydrate) and steamed broccoli (fibre and micronutrients) moves the balance in the right direction.

Key Fact

Target energy split: protein 15%, fat 35% or less, carbohydrate 50% (of which maximum 5% from free sugars, 45% from starches, lactose and fruit sugars). These are the exact figures the written paper may ask for directly.

Carrying Out Nutritional Analysis

Nutritional analysis means calculating how much energy and how many nutrients a recipe or meal provides per serving. In a school kitchen or professional setting this is done using nutritional analysis software (e.g. Nutritionix, Cronometer or bespoke food-technology software). In an exam, it is done using food tables (printed tables of nutritional values per 100 g for each ingredient).

The method is: identify each ingredient and its weight in the recipe; look up its nutritional values per 100 g in the food table; scale to the actual weight used (e.g. if the table gives values per 100 g and you use 250 g, multiply by 2.5); add up all the ingredient contributions to get the total for the whole recipe; then divide by the number of portions to get the value per serving. This can be done for energy (kcal), protein (g), fat (g), carbohydrate (g), fibre (g), and individual vitamins or minerals.

Once you have the analysis, you can compare it to the Dietary Reference Values (DRVs) or Reference Intakes (RIs) for the target person and identify nutrients that are too high or too low. If the recipe is too high in saturated fat, you might substitute full-fat cream for a lower-fat yoghurt, or grill the meat instead of frying. If it is low in iron, you could add spinach, kidney beans or fortified cereal to the recipe.

The written paper may present a recipe analysis and ask you to suggest modifications. The key is to apply the energy percentages and RIs as benchmarks. Common modifications: (1) Too much saturated fat — swap butter for an unsaturated spread or olive oil; use skimmed or semi-skimmed milk instead of full-fat; remove the skin from chicken before cooking. (2) Too much salt — use herbs and spices to season instead of added salt; choose low-salt stock cubes; reduce the amount of processed ingredients. (3) Too little fibre — swap white pasta for wholemeal; add lentils or beans; include more vegetables. (4) Too much free sugar — reduce the amount of added sugar; use fresh fruit to sweeten instead of syrup or jam. Each modification should be linked back to a specific health benefit.
exam_tip_html: Calculation questions are assessed via 2 marks — State / Give or 4 marks — Explain, and the mark scheme rewards method as well as the correct answer. Always show your working: if you multiply the wrong number but your calculation method is correct, you may still earn a method mark. A common error is forgetting to scale the food table value to the actual amount used — food tables give values per 100 g, but a recipe may use 350 g of an ingredient. Always multiply (amount used ÷ 100) × (value per 100 g). For the recommended energy percentages, the most frequently tested figures are: protein 15%, fat 35% or less, carbohydrate 50%, free sugars maximum 5%. If a question asks you to “analyse” or “evaluate” a recipe’s nutritional profile, use these benchmarks explicitly and then suggest a specific, justified modification.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • BMR is the energy needed at rest; it is affected by age, gender, body composition, hormones and life stage. PAL reflects activity level. Total energy need = BMR × PAL. Energy balance means intake equals expenditure.
  • Recommended energy proportions: protein 15%, fat 35% or less, carbohydrate 50% (with a maximum 5% from free sugars). These benchmarks are the basis for evaluating and modifying recipes.
  • Nutritional analysis uses food tables or software to calculate the energy and nutrients in a recipe per serving. Findings are compared to Dietary Reference Values and used to justify recipe modifications.

practice_questions.text:
What does PAL stand for?
A. Physical Activity Level
B. Protein Absorption Limit
C. Personal Allowance Index
D. Physical Analysis Limit
State the recommended percentage of total energy that should come from fat in a balanced diet.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: 35% or less (accept 'no more than 35%').

practice_questions.text: A recipe uses 200 g of cheddar cheese. A food table shows that cheddar provides 1.6 g of calcium per 100 g. Calculate the total calcium provided by the cheese in this recipe. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct method: (200 ÷ 100) × 1.6 = 2 × 1.6; 1 mark for correct answer: 3.2 g of calcium. Accept the answer with or without the unit if the working clearly shows it.

practice_questions.text: Describe three factors that affect a person's basal metabolic rate (BMR).
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any three distinct, correctly described factors: age (BMR decreases with age as muscle mass declines and metabolism slows); gender (males typically have a higher BMR because of greater muscle mass); body composition/muscle mass (more muscle tissue means a higher BMR because muscle burns more energy at rest than fat tissue); hormones (e.g. an overactive thyroid raises BMR); life stage/pregnancy (BMR increases during pregnancy). Up to 3 marks.

practice_questions.text: Jabir is a 17-year-old who plays football twice a week and cycles to college every day. He is trying to understand why he needs more energy than his 17-year-old cousin who works from home and rarely exercises. Explain how BMR and PAL together determine Jabir's higher energy requirement.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 2 marks per developed explanation. (1) BMR: even at rest, Jabir may have a higher BMR than his cousin because regular exercise builds lean muscle mass; muscle burns more energy at rest than fat, so his resting metabolic rate is elevated (1 mark point; 1 mark reason/consequence). (2) PAL: Jabir's daily cycling and football sessions mean his PAL multiplier is significantly higher (1.7 or above vs a sedentary 1.4); because total energy = BMR × PAL, even a modest difference in PAL compounds to a large difference in total daily requirement (1 mark point; 1 mark development using the formula). 1 mark for identification; 1 mark for developed reasoning, per point.

practice_questions.text: Nadia is planning to modify a beef lasagne recipe to reduce its saturated fat content while keeping it nutritionally balanced. She carries out a nutritional analysis and finds that one portion provides 22 g of saturated fat, which exceeds the recommended daily maximum of 20 g. Evaluate two modifications Nadia could make to reduce the saturated fat content, considering both the nutritional impact and the effect on the sensory properties of the finished dish.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9 marks): Identifies two well-chosen modifications (e.g. 1: swap beef mince for extra-lean mince or substitute half with lentils/TVP; 2: replace full-fat creme fraiche or cheese topping with a lower-fat bechamel using semi-skimmed milk and a reduced amount of cheddar, or use a ricotta-based layer). For each modification, analyses both the nutritional impact (quantitative or descriptive: how much saturated fat is saved; which other nutrients are affected positively or negatively) AND the sensory effect (texture, flavour, appearance — e.g. removing full-fat cheese reduces the creamy, rich mouthfeel and golden top; lentils add a slightly earthy flavour and denser texture). Accurate use of saturated fat, BMI, energy density, palatability and reference intake vocabulary. Analysis is not merely descriptive but examines relationships and consequences.

Secure (5–7 marks): Identifies two modifications with reasonable development of either nutritional or sensory impact (not necessarily both for each). Mostly accurate. Some analysis of relationships.

Developing (3–4 marks): Identifies modifications but gives only descriptive rather than analytical treatment. Little examination of sensory consequences or the interplay between fat reduction and palatability.

Emerging (1–2 marks): Names a modification (e.g. 'use less cheese') with no analysis of the nutritional or sensory consequences.

flashcard_questions.q: What does BMR stand for and what does it measure?
flashcard_questions.a: Basal metabolic rate — the energy needed at rest to maintain vital body functions.

flashcard_questions.q: What is PAL and how is it used?
flashcard_questions.a: Physical activity level — a multiplier applied to BMR to calculate total daily energy need.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the formula for calculating total daily energy requirement?
flashcard_questions.a: Total energy = BMR multiplied by PAL.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does a person with more muscle mass have a higher BMR?
flashcard_questions.a: Muscle tissue burns more energy at rest than fat tissue does.
When daily energy intake equals daily energy expenditure, keeping body weight stable.

flashcard_questions.q: What percentage of total energy should come from protein?
What is the maximum percentage of total energy that should come from fat?
What is the maximum percentage of total energy from free sugars?
How do you scale a food table value to the amount used in a recipe?
flashcard_questions.a: Divide the weight used by 100, then multiply by the value per 100 g.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a food table show that makes nutritional analysis possible?
flashcard_questions.a: The energy and nutrient content of each food per 100 g.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does BMR decline with age?
flashcard_questions.a: Muscle mass decreases and metabolism slows as the body ages.

flashcard_questions.q: How would you modify a recipe that is too high in saturated fat to reduce it without losing protein?
flashcard_questions.a: Swap full-fat dairy for lower-fat alternatives or replace some red meat with lentils or TVP.

glossary_terms.definition: The minimum amount of energy the body needs at complete rest to maintain vital functions such as breathing, heartbeat, temperature regulation and organ function.
A multiplier applied to BMR that reflects how active a person is throughout the day; used to calculate total daily energy requirement.
The state in which daily energy intake from food and drink equals daily energy expenditure through BMR and physical activity, resulting in a stable body weight.
The process of calculating the energy and nutrient content of a recipe or diet using food tables or software, and comparing the results to dietary reference values.
Government-issued benchmarks for the amounts of energy and specific nutrients needed by different groups of people to maintain good health.
